title: The prisoner's dilemma
src: Flood and Dresher, RAND, 1950; named by Albert Tucker
idea: Two people each gain by cheating, yet both end up worse off than if they had cooperated. Self interest alone can produce a bad result for everyone.
apply: When you spot a trap where everyone is tempted to cut corners, change the rules so cooperation pays.
who: Rae and Jo, roommates who both skip the dishes.

scenes.cap: Rae and Jo's choice, every night

items.x: Skipping is free, if the other washes

scenes.nar: Rae and Jo share a kitchen. Washing up costs fifteen minutes. Skipping is free, as long as the other person washes.

items: If Jo skips, I skip too

scenes.nar: Whatever Jo does, Rae is better off skipping, and Jo reasons the same. So both skip, and the kitchen is a mess, which is worse for both than sharing the work.

items.x: A simple rota on the fridge

scenes.nar: Game theory calls this the prisoner's dilemma. The fix is to change the payoffs. They post a rota, and whoever skips owes a coffee.

items.x: Skipping is rare, and owned up to

scenes.nar: The kitchen stays clean, the resentment fades, and skipping becomes rare. Cooperation now pays.
